cards.name: The 'So what?' test
cards.summary: After every claim, ask 'So what?' as the busiest, most sceptical reader would, and keep answering until you reach something that reader already cares about (money, time, risk, status, a named problem from the brief); that answer becomes the line and the original claim becomes its proof. Good copy keeps the chain true: every link is something the product actually does.
use_for: turning a client's feature list into landing-page and sales-page benefits
B2B one-pagers and decks where every slide states a spec ('ISO 27001 certified', 'API-first')
cold emails and LinkedIn DMs where one line must earn the reply
founder posts and press notes that open with what the company did instead of why the reader should care
self-editing any draft: a sentence with no 'so what' answer is a cut candidate
avoid: Chaining past what you can prove ('auto-reconciliation, which means peace of mind, which means you can finally relax'): stop at the first benefit the client can back with a fact or a customer story.
Spec-led readers (procurement teams, developers, data sheets, tenders): they need the spec itself; keep the spec first and add the 'which means' after it, not instead of it.

Regulated categories (health, finance, insurance, education results): the end of the chain is often an outcome claim you are not allowed to make; stop where the claim is still substantiated and check comp:asci_code before publishing.
how: Write the claim the way the client says it: the feature, the credential, the fact ('Our software auto-reconciles purchase invoices with GSTR-2B').
Read it as one specific reader from the brief (a Surat textile trader, a first-time mutual fund investor) and ask 'So what?' (in Hinglish briefs: 'Toh? Isse mujhe kya?').
Answer in one sentence that starts 'which means...'. Ask 'So what?' of that answer.

Stop when the answer names something the reader already feels without being told: rupees saved or lost, hours, a penalty or notice avoided, a person they care about, how they look to their boss or family. Two or three rounds is normal; if you need five, the claim probably does not matter to this reader: cut it.
Check every link with the client: each 'which means' must be true for this product. If a link needs a number, ask for it rather than estimating.
Write the last true answer as the line, and put the original claim right after it as the reason ('..., because it matches every bill to GSTR-2B as you upload it').
Repeat for each feature, then compare the answers: if three features all end in 'saves time', keep the strongest and merge or drop the rest.
cards.before: Our GST software auto-reconciles purchase invoices with GSTR-2B.
cards.after: See every supplier bill that won't count for input tax credit before you file, not after the notice comes. Our software matches each bill to GSTR-2B as you upload it.
overuse_signs: Every feature has been turned into an emotion ('freedom', 'peace of mind') and the concrete specs have vanished
The same end benefit ('save time', 'grow your business') repeated for every feature
'Which means' left in the published copy again and again as a verbal tic
Benefits that the client cannot substantiate, invented to finish the chain

sources.title: Handcart Media: the 'So what' test for website copy
sources.supports: practitioner description of the test (secondary, low confidence; folk technique with no single originator)

cards.name: Social proof
cards.summary: Show the reader that people like them have already chosen this (customer counts, ratings, named users, client logos, community size) so the decision feels safe. Good social proof is real, specific, attributable and drawn from people who resemble the reader, and it sits where the reader hesitates.
use_for: landing pages, sales pages and pricing pages next to the CTA
subject lines and ad headlines built on a real count ('1,240 Pune parents use this checklist')
B2B pages and decks via client logos and named case studies (with permission)
reels and WhatsApp broadcasts that show real reviews or customer clips
public-service and civic copy that tells people how many neighbours already did the right thing
avoid: Invented, inflated or rounded-up numbers, fake or AI-written reviews, or logos used without permission: this is a compliance and trust failure, not a style choice (see comp:ftc_consumer_reviews_rule, comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022, comp:asci_code). Use a smaller true number or a different proof type.
Shaming copy that tells readers most people do the wrong thing ('Most Indians never check their credit score'): it makes the wrong behaviour sound normal. State how many do the right thing instead.
Proof from people unlike the reader (a Fortune 500 logo on a page for Jaipur kirana owners): find proof from the reader's city, role, size or problem, or use authority proof instead.
Small counts presented as big ones ('Join 37 users!'): use a rate, a named story or a guarantee until the count is persuasive.
how: Inventory the real proof with the client: customer or user count (with date), ratings (score, number of reviews, platform), repeat-purchase or renewal data, named customers who agreed to be quoted, client logos with permission, press mentions, community size. Note the source and date of each in your working file.
Pick the proof that matches the reader: same city, same role, same business size, same problem. '38 home bakers in Pune' beats '10,000+ users' for a Pune home baker.
Make it specific and checkable: number + unit + time window + where it comes from ('4.6 on Google from 1,240 reviews, as of Sept 2026'). Never round up.

Choose the form for the channel: a count in a subject line or headline; a named quote with photo on a landing page; a screenshot of a real WhatsApp or Google review in a reel (with the customer's consent); logos and a case-study link in B2B.
Place it at the moment of doubt: beside the CTA, under the price, next to the sign-up form, and right after the boldest claim (see tech:testimonial_placement).
Keep the substantiation file (claim, source, date) with the draft so the client can answer an ASCI or platform query.
cards.before: Trusted by thousands of happy customers across India.
cards.after: 412 home bakers in Pune re-ordered our 5 kg flour pack within a month. (Our Shopify order data, July to August 2026.)
overuse_signs: Proof in every paragraph, so the reader stops noticing it
Vanity numbers that have nothing to do with the decision ('1 million impressions')
Counts with no source, date or platform
'Join thousands of...' boilerplate pasted onto every page and email
Review walls with only first names and five stars, which read as fake

sources.title: Cialdini: Seven Principles of Persuasion (Influence at Work)
sources.supports: social proof / consensus is one of Cialdini's principles of persuasion

sources.title: Social proof (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and research background

cards.name: Specificity
cards.summary: Replace vague words with exact, checkable details (counts, rupee amounts, names, places, times, a concrete instance of the category) so the reader can picture the claim and believe it. Good specificity is always true and sourced; an invented exact number is worse than an honest vague one.
use_for: headlines, hooks and subject lines that need to stop a scroll
service pages and case studies that otherwise say 'many clients' and 'great results'
cold emails where one concrete detail proves you did your homework
news, scheme and civic explainers (who, which district, how much, by when)
bios, CVs and proposals ('managed a Rs 2 crore annual ad budget', not 'large budgets')
avoid: False precision: inventing '97.3%' or '2,341 clients' to sound credible. If the client has no number, ask for it; if it does not exist, write the true plain claim or cut it.
Specifics that leak confidential client data (revenue, names, contracts) without written permission: anonymise ('a Jaipur jewellery exporter') but keep the numbers you are allowed to use.
Outcome numbers in regulated categories (weight loss, returns, exam results) without substantiation: they become claims a regulator can challenge (comp:asci_code, comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022).
Units the reader cannot decode (CAC, ROAS, TAT) in consumer copy: translate into rupees, days or people.
how: Underline every vague word in the draft: many, several, lots, leading, top, best, quality, affordable, fast, soon, huge, solutions, various.
For each, ask the question it dodges: how many? which ones? where? by when? how much in rupees? compared to what?
Get the answer from the brief, the client or a source, and write it down with where it came from.
Replace the vague word with count + unit + time window ('212 CA firms in 9 months'), a named place ('Malviya Nagar, Jaipur'), a time ('delivered by 1 pm'), or a price ('Rs 1,180 a month').
Swap category words for one concrete instance: 'healthy snacks' becomes 'roasted makhana, no palm oil'; 'small businesses' becomes 'two-chair salons'.
Keep the exact figure you have; do not round 1,180 up to 'over 1,000' or 'thousands'.
Limit to one or two specifics per sentence; a line with four numbers blurs. Move extra detail to a table or the next sentence.
Run edit:fact_check on every specific before the draft leaves you.
cards.before: We help many businesses grow quickly with our affordable digital marketing solutions.
cards.after: We run Google Ads for 31 dental clinics in Jaipur. Last quarter the median clinic got 46 booked appointments on Rs 18,000 of ad spend.
overuse_signs: Every sentence carries a number, so none stands out
Statistics with no source, date or sample
Decimals on what are really estimates ('saves 3.7 hours')
Strings of names, places and figures that do not support the point being made

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 12: use definite, specific, concrete language

cards.name: Step-by-step instructions
cards.summary: Write a procedure as a numbered list under a heading that says what the reader will get done, one action per step, each step a complete sentence that starts with where to act or an imperative verb, ending with the action that completes the task. Good steps can be followed with the product open in the other hand and no rereading.
use_for: help-centre and knowledge-base articles
user manuals, SOPs and onboarding guides
how-to blog posts and developer tutorials
WhatsApp support replies and in-app tooltips that walk a user through a setting
voice-over scripts for screen-recording tutorials (one step per spoken sentence)
avoid: Numbering things that are not a sequence (features, tips, options): use a bulleted list (tech:bulleted_lists).
A single action dressed up as '1.': write it as one sentence or a single bullet.
Explanations, warnings and background crammed into steps: put the 'why' before the list and a short result line after it, and keep only the action in the step.
Procedures so long the reader loses their place: split into named sub-tasks ('Set up your account', 'Add your first invoice') each with its own short list.
how: Write a heading that names the task as the reader would ('Add your GSTIN to invoices'), parallel with the other headings on the page ('Add...', 'Change...', 'Delete...').
Only add an intro sentence if it says something the heading does not (who can do this, what you need ready).
List every action in order on paper first, by actually doing the task in the product or watching the SME do it.
One action per step; combine two short actions only when they happen in the same place on screen.
Start each step with where to act if there is any chance of confusion ('In Settings, ...', 'On the Invoices tab, ...'), otherwise with an imperative verb (Open, Select, Enter, Copy).
Use the exact on-screen label, in bold, and say where it is before what to do with it ('For GSTIN, enter...').
Write each step as a complete sentence: capital letter, full stop.
Include the step that finishes the task (Select Save, Select Submit), then one line saying what the reader now sees or can do.
Test it: follow your own steps literally on a fresh account. Any step you had to guess becomes a rewrite.
cards.before: To add a GST number to your invoices, you should go to settings, where you will find the business profile section in which the GSTIN can be entered, after which it should be saved and it will then appear.
cards.after:
Add your GSTIN to invoices
1. Go to Settings > Business profile.
2. In GSTIN, enter your 15-character GST number.
3. Select Save.
Your GSTIN now prints on every new invoice.
overuse_signs: Every paragraph on the page is a numbered list, including explanations and opinions
Steps that only say 'Click Next' ten times because nothing was combined
Steps with three or four actions joined by 'and then'
Numbered lists inside numbered lists more than one level deep

sources.title: Microsoft Writing Style Guide: Writing step-by-step instructions
sources.supports: numbered list for multi-step procedures; separate step per instruction; start with location or an imperative verb; complete sentences; include the completing action; parallel headings (read 2026-10-05)

cards.name: Subject line + preheader pairing
cards.summary: Write the preheader (preview text) as the second half of the subject line: it adds the detail, proof or payoff the subject sets up, never repeats it, and is set deliberately so the inbox does not pull in 'View this email in your browser'. Good pairs read as one sentence in the inbox: sender, subject, preheader.
use_for: promotional and launch emails
newsletters, where the preheader can list what else is inside
welcome, nurture and win-back sequences
transactional emails, where the preheader carries the key detail (amount, date, order number)
avoid: A preheader that repeats the subject ('Diwali sale is live' / 'Our Diwali sale is now live'): use the space for the offer detail or the reason to open now.
A subject that promises what the email does not deliver, with the preheader doubling down: deceptive subject lines are a legal issue as well as a trust one (comp:can_spam); make both match the body.
Personalisation tokens with no fallback ('Hi , your offer'): set a fallback value or leave the token out (tech:personalization_tokens).
Leaving the preheader blank: the inbox fills it with the first text in the email, often a browser link, alt text or legal boilerplate.
how: Write the subject first: it carries the one reason to open, with the key words at the start (character guidance lives in plat:email_subject_line).
Write the preheader as the next sentence of the same thought. Pick one job: add the specific detail (price, date, place), pay off or deepen a curiosity subject, add proof, or say what to do.
Do not reuse the subject's words; if you have to, the subject is doing too much.
Front-load the preheader too: mobile inboxes show only the start, so the useful words go first.
Read sender name + subject + preheader aloud as one line; it should sound like one person talking.
Set the preheader in your email tool's preview-text field, or as hidden text placed right after the opening body tag, so the inbox does not pull body copy.
Send a test to Gmail (app and web) and an iPhone and check what actually shows before scheduling.
cards.before:
Subject: Diwali sale is live
Preheader: View this email in your browser
cards.after:
Subject: Your Diwali gifting, sorted
Preheader: Brass diyas and dry-fruit hampers, shipped from Jaipur in 2 days. 20% off till Sunday.
overuse_signs: Every preheader is a teaser question, so none of them carry information
Emoji or 'Open now!' padding the preheader instead of content
Preheaders written once and reused across a whole sequence
Subject and preheader that only make sense if the reader sees both, on clients that show only one

sources.title: Litmus: The ultimate guide to preview text
sources.supports: without set preview text, inboxes pull the first lines of copy (e.g. 'View this email in your browser'); preview text should extend the subject, not repeat it; hidden-div method (read 2026-10-05)

cards.name: Swipe file
cards.summary: Keep an organised collection of copy that worked (ads, emails, landing pages, hooks, scripts), each saved with its context and tagged by the move it makes, and study it for structure before you write. Good use of a swipe file borrows the move and the order of parts, never the sentences.
use_for: starting a genre you have not written before (study 5-10 examples' structure first)
hook and headline bake-offs: pull every saved hook of one type and write your own versions
pitching clients ('here are three directions, each based on a pattern that has run for months')
training a junior writer or an AI writer on what good looks like in a niche
avoid: Rewording a swiped line ('The shoes that think for your feet' to 'The bag that thinks for your back'): that is close paraphrase, a copyright and reputation risk; take the structure and write from the client's own facts.
Swiping across markets and awareness levels (a long US supplement letter for an Indian B2B SaaS buyer): pull swipes for the same reader, price point and awareness level.
Treating 'famous' as 'works now': classic ads are for learning moves; check the current channel's top performers too.
Collecting without tagging: an untagged folder of 900 screenshots is never opened. Tag by move as you save.
how: Collect from copy someone paid to test: emails you opened, ads you keep seeing (long-running ads in the Meta Ad Library are a good sign), competitor landing and pricing pages, top reels and posts in the client's niche, and classic ads studied by name.
Save each with context: link, date, channel, the audience you think it targets, the job it is doing, and one line on what stopped you.
Tag by move, not by brand: 'hook: number list', 'guarantee', 'objection answered in FAQ', 'Hinglish CTA', 'price anchor'.
Before drafting, pull 5-10 swipes of the same genre and awareness level and write down only their skeleton: the parts in order and what each part does.
Close the swipe file. Draft from the skeleton using the client's facts, customer words and offer.
After drafting, compare against the swipes: any phrase that echoes one gets rewritten; run edit:plagiarism_check on long pieces.
Prune quarterly: delete swipes you can no longer explain.
cards.before: Swiped line, reworded: 'The bag that thinks for your back.'
cards.after: Move taken from the swipe: name the reader's exact moment of pain. Own line: 'Built for the 8:40 Andheri fast, when your laptop bag takes a shoulder at every station.'
overuse_signs: Drafts that feel like a remix of one famous ad
Every piece follows the same swiped template, whatever the brief
Hours spent collecting, minutes spent writing
Lines that a client or competitor recognises as someone else's

sources.title: Swipe file (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: collection of tested copy kept for reference

cards.name: Testimonial placement
cards.summary: Put each specific, named testimonial directly beside the claim it proves or the objection it answers (under the price, next to 'will this work for me?', above the CTA) instead of collecting all of them in a block at the end. Good placement means a doubting reader meets the right customer's words at the exact moment the doubt appears.
use_for: landing pages and sales pages
pricing pages (a quote about value right under the price)
service pages for agencies, CA firms, clinics and coaches
case-study-led emails and proposals
reels and VSLs (a short customer clip right after the claim on screen)
avoid: Anonymous or initials-only quotes ('R.S., Delhi'): get a full name, role or city, and a photo where permitted, or do not use it.
Editing a quote until it says something the customer did not mean: trim for length only, keep their words, and get their approval of the final version.
Paid, gifted or incentivised testimonials without disclosure, or atypical results shown as typical: disclose the relationship and the typical result (comp:ftc_endorsement_guides, comp:asci_code).
A generic quote ('Great service, highly recommend!') next to a specific claim: it proves nothing; find one that names the result or the objection.
how: List the page's claims and the reader's objections in the order the page meets them (does it work, will it work for someone like me, is it worth the price, is it hard to start, can I trust you).

For each, find the testimonial that proves exactly that point: one that names the before state, the objection or the result. Ask the client for more customer quotes if a slot is empty; do not invent one.
Trim the quote to the one or two sentences that do that job, in the customer's words, and send the trimmed version to the customer for approval.
Attach full attribution: name, role or business, city, and the plan or product they used.
Place it immediately after the claim or beside the objection, and put the strongest value quote under the price or above the main CTA.
Keep a review wall or carousel lower down for readers who want more, as a second placement, not the only one.
Check the page top to bottom: every major claim has its proof within one scroll.
cards.before: [Hero] > [Features] > [Pricing: Rs 4,999 a year] > [Buy now] > [Footer: 'What our customers say', 12 reviews in a carousel]
cards.after: [Pricing: Rs 4,999 a year] > right below: 'I thought Rs 4,999 was a lot for a 3-person office. It paid for itself in the first GST quarter.' Mehul Shah, partner, Shah & Co., Surat > [Buy now]
overuse_signs: A testimonial after every paragraph, so the page reads like a review site
The same quote repeated in three places
Long testimonials that bury the one sentence that matters
Quotes chosen for the famous name rather than the point they prove

sources.title: Testimonial (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: what a testimonial is in advertising

cards.name: Title tag writing
cards.summary: Write a unique, descriptive, concise <title> for every page that says what the page is in the words a searcher uses, with the brand added briefly; no keyword lists and no boilerplate repeated across pages. Good titles front-load the meaning, because search results truncate long titles to fit the screen and Google may rewrite titles that are vague or stuffed.
use_for: service, product and category pages
blog posts and guides (the title tag can differ from the on-page H1)
local business pages ('GST registration in Jaipur')
programmatic SEO templates, where the variable parts must make each title unique
avoid: Keyword stuffing ('CA Jaipur | Best CA Jaipur | Chartered Accountant Jaipur'): write one natural phrase that describes the page.
The same boilerplate on every page ('Home | Mehta & Associates'): make each title say what that page is.
Clickbait titles the page does not deliver: Google may replace the title, and readers bounce; promise exactly what the page answers.
A long brand slogan on every title: brand concisely ('| Mehta & Associates') or leave it to the homepage.
how: Write down what the page is and who searches for it, in the searcher's words (check the query phrasing with tech:search_intent_matching).
Put the main topic first: service or subject, then the qualifier that makes it specific (city, year, audience, format).
Add the brand at the end, short, after a separator ('| Mehta & Associates'); skip it if the title is already long.
Keep it concise enough that the meaning survives if the end is cut off; Google sets no hard length but truncates to the device width.
Make each title unique across the site: list all titles in a sheet and look for duplicates and near-duplicates.
Make sure the title, the H1 and the most visible heading on the page agree about what the page is.
After publishing, check the live result in Google; if Google rewrote it, the title was probably vague, stuffed or out of step with the page.
cards.before: Best CA Jaipur | CA in Jaipur | Chartered Accountant Jaipur | Tax Filing Jaipur | Home
cards.after: GST Registration and Return Filing in Jaipur | Mehta & Associates
overuse_signs: Every title follows the same '[Keyword] | [Keyword variant] | [Brand]' template
Year stamps ('2026') on pages that are not updated
Brackets, caps and emoji added to every title to grab clicks
Titles rewritten weekly chasing rank changes

sources.title: Google Search Central: Influencing your title links
sources.supports: every page needs a title; descriptive and concise; avoid keyword stuffing; avoid repeated or boilerplate text; brand concisely; no length limit but titles are truncated to device width; Google may generate title links from other sources (read 2026-10-05)

cards.name: TL;DR / key-takeaways summary
cards.summary: Open a long piece with a short summary (two or three sentences, or three to five bullets) that gives the actual answers: what the reader will learn, what was decided, or what they must do and by when. A good TL;DR lets a reader who stops there act correctly; the body is the evidence.
use_for: internal memos, policy updates and announcements
reports, white papers and research summaries (as an executive summary)
long blog posts, guides and explainers (a key-takeaways box under the intro)
newsletters that cover several items
page summaries and meta-style descriptions on information sites
avoid: Table-of-contents summaries that list topics ('Background, options, next steps'): write the conclusion of each topic instead.
Teaser summaries that hold back the answer to make people read on: give the answer; curiosity belongs in headlines, not summaries.
Short pieces (a 150-word post or email) with a TL;DR on top: the piece is already the summary; cut it.
A summary that says something the body does not support, or misses the one action the reader must take.
how: Finish the draft first, then write the summary from what the piece actually says.
Decide which job it does: 'what you will learn' (guides), 'what was decided and why' (memos, reports), or 'what you must do by when' (announcements, policy).
Write two or three sentences or three to five bullets. Each bullet is a full claim with its specific (number, date, name), not a topic label.
Put the action and its deadline first if there is one.
Do not repeat the headline's words; add what the headline could not hold.
Place it right under the headline or opening line, above the fold.
On long web pages, link each takeaway to its section.
Test: give only the summary to someone; can they say what changed and what to do? If not, rewrite it.
cards.before: TL;DR: This memo covers the background to our payroll timing review, the options we considered, and next steps.
cards.after: TL;DR: From November, salaries are paid on the last working day of the month instead of the 1st. The amount does not change. If an EMI leaves your account between the 1st and 5th, tell HR by 20 October and we'll pay you early once.
overuse_signs: A TL;DR on every post regardless of length
Takeaways boxes that repeat the subheads word for word
Bullet summaries longer than the sections they summarise
'In this article, we will explore...' openers labelled as a summary

sources.title: GOV.UK: Write clear summaries
sources.supports: summaries say clearly what the content is about so users can judge relevance; do not repeat the title; GOV.UK page summaries are kept to 160 characters including spaces and end with a full stop (read 2026-10-05)

cards.name: Topic and entity coverage
cards.summary: Plan a page so it answers the main question plus the sub-questions a real reader asks next, and names the entities (forms, laws, tools, places, organisations, numbers) a complete answer needs. Good coverage makes the page sufficient on its own for that intent; it is measured by reader questions answered, not by word count or a competitor's length.
use_for: pillar pages, ultimate guides and how-to articles
service and local pages that must answer 'how much, how long, what do I need'
content briefs for other writers
content refreshes of pages that rank but do not satisfy
pages meant to be cited by AI answers and AI overviews
avoid: Padding to match a competitor's word count: cover what readers need, then stop.
Dropping in lists of 'LSI' or 'NLP keywords' without explaining them: each entity named must be used to answer something.
Covering a neighbouring intent on the same page (a 'GST registration' guide that also teaches GST return filing in full): link to a separate page instead (fw:topic_cluster).
History and definition sections that no searcher at this intent wants ('What is GST? History of GST'): open with the answer.
how: Write the page's one main question and the searcher's intent in a sentence (see tech:search_intent_matching).

List the next questions a real reader asks: from People Also Ask, autocomplete, Reddit and Quora threads, the client's support tickets and sales calls, and the headings of the pages that currently rank.
List the entities a complete answer must name: forms, portals, laws, documents, tools, organisations, places, thresholds, costs, timelines. Verify each from a primary source.
Group questions into sections in the order a reader needs them; drop questions that belong to another intent and link to them instead.
Answer each sub-question directly in the first sentence of its section (tech:answer_first_paragraph), then give the detail and the source.
Add what the ranking pages lack: first-hand experience, a worked example, real numbers from the client, a local detail (tech:eeat_first_hand_experience).
Final check: every section answers a reader question; no section exists only for length or a keyword.
cards.before: Outline for 'GST registration for freelancers': What is GST? / History of GST in India / Benefits of GST / Conclusion
cards.after: Outline for 'GST registration for freelancers': Do freelancers need GST registration? / Documents you need before you apply / Applying on the GST portal, step by step / Billing foreign clients: export of services and the LUT / How long it takes and what it costs / What happens if you don't register
overuse_signs: Articles that answer every possible question about a topic and so serve no single reader
Glossary-style paragraphs defining terms the reader already knows
Long FAQ blocks repeating what the body already said
Word counts creeping up with every refresh while answers get harder to find

sources.title: Google Search Central: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
sources.supports: asks whether the content gives a substantial, complete or comprehensive description of the topic

sources.title: Semantic search (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: search engines matching meaning and entities, not only keywords

cards.name: Transitions
cards.summary: Signal the logical link between sentences and paragraphs (contrast, cause, example, sequence, addition) so the reader never wonders why the next part follows. Good transitions are mostly carried by the logic itself (a repeated key word, a question the last line raised, a short 'But' or 'So'), not by stacked connector words.
use_for: articles, reports and white papers with a multi-step argument
sales pages and long emails that move from problem to proof to offer
scripts and VO, where the listener cannot glance back
LinkedIn posts and newsletters made of short paragraphs that must still read as one thought
avoid: Stacking 'Moreover', 'Furthermore', 'Additionally' to glue unrelated points: it is a common AI tell (edit:ai_tell_removal). Name the real link or make the points a list.
Adding transitions to hide a structure problem: if you cannot say how paragraph B follows from A, reorder or cut (edit:reverse_outline) before touching the wording.
Throat-clearing transitions ('That being said', 'With that in mind', 'In conclusion'): cut them; the next sentence can start with its point.
how: Reverse-outline the draft: one line per paragraph saying what it does.
Between each pair, write the one-word relationship: and, but, so, because, for example, then. If you cannot name one, the order is wrong: move or cut the paragraph first.

Pick the lightest signal that carries the relationship: a short opener (But, So, Then, For example, That's why), or a built-in link: repeat the key noun from the previous paragraph's last sentence, or answer the question it raised.
Put the signal at the start of the paragraph's first sentence, where the reader looks for it.
Match register: 'However' and 'Therefore' in reports and policy; 'But', 'So', 'Here's the catch' in email and social; 'Par', 'Toh', 'Isliye' in Hinglish captions and VO.
Delete any connector that does not mark a change in direction or a cause.
Read only the first sentence of every paragraph in order: together they should tell the argument.
cards.before: Our clinic uses digital X-rays. Moreover, we are open till 9 pm. Furthermore, parking is available. Additionally, we accept most insurance cards.
cards.after: Our clinic uses digital X-rays, so you see your scan on screen in two minutes. And because we're open till 9 pm, you can come straight from work, park in our basement and pay with your insurance card at the desk.
overuse_signs: Consecutive sentences opening with Moreover, Furthermore, Additionally
Every paragraph begins with a connector word
Formal connectors ('Thus', 'Hence') in a casual Instagram caption
'In conclusion' or 'To sum up' before a short ending that needs no announcement

sources.title: UNC Writing Center: Transitions
sources.supports: transitions express logical relationships (similarity, contrast, sequence, cause, example); poor flow is often an organisation problem, checked by reverse outlining (read 2026-10-05)

cards.name: Twist / reveal
cards.summary: Withhold one fact, plant fair clues, and reveal it late so the reader reinterprets everything before it. A good twist feels surprising in the moment and inevitable on a second read: nothing earlier was a lie, the reader simply assumed.
use_for: brand films, TVC and digital ad scripts with a story
short fiction, micro-drama episodes and web series
reels and shorts built to be rewatched (the reveal sends viewers back to the start)
fundraising and social-cause stories where the reveal is who the person is
LinkedIn and newsletter stories with a payoff line
avoid: Informational content (how-tos, news, scheme explainers, policy): the reader needs the answer first; use tech:answer_first_paragraph instead.
Twists that only work because the setup stated something false: the reader feels cheated and stops trusting the brand. Let them assume; never assert.

Ad reveals that turn the earlier claim into a misleading one (a 'real customer' who turns out to be an actor, a price that changes at the reveal): that is a compliance problem (comp:asci_code), not a twist.
Announcing the twist ('Wait for the twist!'): it tells the reader to look for it, and they will guess.
how: Pick the one fact to withhold: who the narrator is, where we are, when it is, what the object is, who did it.
Write the reveal line first: short, plain, placed at the end (last line, last slide, last 2-3 seconds of a reel).
Write the setup so every line is true both before and after the reveal. Read it twice, once as a first-time reader, once knowing the reveal.
Plant two or three clues that read one way now and another way after the reveal.
Steer the default assumption with what you leave out (no age, no name, no place), never with a false statement.
Give the reveal its own beat: a line break, a cut, a pause in the VO. Cut everything after it except one short line or the CTA.
Test on someone cold: if they guess by the middle, hide a clue better; if they say 'that's not fair', add a clue.
cards.before: Meet Kamla ji, 68, who learnt to pay bills on UPI last month at our free phone classes in Indore.
cards.after: She checks the amount twice. Asks the shopkeeper to wait. Types the PIN slowly, one digit at a time. The payment goes through, and she laughs out loud. Kamla ji is 68. A month ago she had never held a smartphone.
overuse_signs: Every reel or post ends on 'but here's the twist'
Twists the audience predicts from the thumbnail or title
Reveals that depend on a detail never planted
Story after story built on the same reveal type (it was the grandmother all along)

sources.title: Plot twist (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and types of twist

cards.name: Unhide verbs (fix nominalisations)
cards.summary: Find verbs that have been turned into nouns ('make a decision', 'conduct an analysis', 'the implementation of') and turn them back into verbs ('decide', 'analyse', 'implement'), usually putting the doer in front at the same time. Good results are shorter sentences that say who does what.
use_for: government press notes, scheme explainers and circulars
corporate memos, policies and annual reports
proposals, RFP responses and consulting decks
academic and research summaries written for a general reader
Hindi official-style copy ('nirnay liya gaya hai', 'jaanch ki jayegi')
avoid: Terms of art and named things: 'the assessment year', 'GST registration', 'the investigation' as the topic of a paragraph are fine as nouns.
Legal documents with defined terms ('the Disbursement' as defined in clause 2): changing them changes meaning; leave them and simplify around them.
Turning a noun into a verb the reader does not use ('to incentivise', 'to operationalise'): pick a plain verb instead (reward, start).
how: Scan for noun endings that hide a verb: -tion, -sion, -ment, -ance, -ence, -al, and '-ing of' ('the processing of').
Find the weak verb carrying it: make, give, provide, conduct, carry out, perform, undertake, take, have, be. 'Make a decision', 'provide assistance', 'give consideration to'.
Turn the noun back into the verb and delete the weak verb plus the extra 'a', 'the' and 'of': 'make a decision on' becomes 'decide'.
Name the doer and put it first; this often fixes a passive at the same time (tech:active_voice).
In Hindi and Hinglish, do the same: 'nirnay liya gaya' becomes 'tay kiya', 'jaanch ki jayegi' becomes '[who] jaanchenge'.
Reread: the sentence should be shorter, and you should be able to point at who acts.
cards.before: The committee will undertake a review of all applications and make a determination regarding eligibility, following which the disbursement of funds will take place.
cards.after: The committee will review every application, decide who is eligible, and then pay out the funds.
overuse_signs: Defined legal or technical terms rewritten into verbs and losing precision
Sentences so stripped they become a string of short verb commands
Jargon verbs coined from nouns ('to solution', 'to dialogue')

sources.title: Nominalization (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: verbs and adjectives turned into nouns

cards.name: Unique mechanism
cards.summary: Name and explain the specific method that makes the result possible (an ingredient, process, design choice, data source or way of working), and contrast it with why the reader's earlier attempts failed, so a sceptical reader believes this one is different. A good mechanism is true, specific to this product, and explainable in two plain sentences.
use_for: sales pages, VSLs and long-form emails for markets that have heard every promise
D2C product pages competing in crowded categories (skincare, supplements, edtech, fintech apps)
B2B pitches where competitors claim the same outcome
ad angles: one ad per mechanism instead of one ad per promise
avoid: Invented pseudo-science or empty names ('Quantum Fat-Lock', 'Proprietary AI Engine'): name what actually happens, in words a buyer can check.
Mechanism claims in health, food, finance and coaching that need substantiation: get the evidence before writing (comp:asci_code, comp:fssai_advertising_claims_2018, comp:ccpa_coaching_ads_2024).

Leading with the mechanism for readers who do not yet feel the problem: establish the problem first (fw:schwartz_awareness_levels); a mechanism pays off most when the market has seen many similar claims (fw:market_sophistication).
Calling a common process unique: if every competitor does it, say why yours is done differently or pick a different angle.
how: Interview the founder or SME: 'Why does this work when the things your customers tried before did not?' Push past the outcome to the cause (tech:sme_interview).
Write the problem mechanism: the specific reason the old way fails the reader ('tuition repeats the chapter louder; the gap is from two classes earlier').
Write the solution mechanism: what this product does differently that removes that cause.
Give it a plain, concrete name if it helps memory ('the 20-minute gap test'), never a name that hides what it is.
Explain it in one or two sentences a 12-year-old could follow, with an analogy or picture if needed.
Order the argument: problem, why earlier fixes failed, the mechanism, the result, the proof.
Check with the client that every part is true and specific to them, and keep the evidence.
cards.before: Our maths classes help every child score better.
cards.after: Most tuition repeats the chapter louder. We start each child with a 20-minute gap test that finds the class-6 idea behind the class-9 mistake, then teach only that for three weeks.
overuse_signs: Every product and every feature gets a capitalised, trademark-style name
Long mechanism explanations before the reader cares about the problem
Mechanism names that mean nothing without a paragraph of explanation
A new 'secret method' launched every campaign for the same product

sources.title: Todd Brown: What's your product's unique mechanism?
sources.supports: definition; promotes the process rather than the result (harvest saw it via search; the URL redirected to a social post on 2026-10-05, low confidence)

sources.title: Unique selling proposition (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: the older USP concept the mechanism builds on

cards.name: Voice-of-customer mining
cards.summary: Collect the exact words customers use about their problem, their failed fixes, their objections and the product (from reviews, support chats, sales calls, comments, surveys, interviews) and write headlines, hooks and FAQs in those words. Good VOC copy sounds like the reader talking, including Hinglish where that is how they talk, while the brand keeps its own voice in the body.
use_for: headlines, hooks and subject lines
landing pages and product pages for D2C brands
ad angle research before a campaign
FAQ blocks and objection handling written as customers actually ask
persona and messaging documents
avoid: Publishing a mined review as a testimonial without the customer's permission, or rewording it into a fake one: ask, attribute, or keep it as research only (comp:ftc_consumer_reviews_rule).
Collecting personal data from private chats, groups or tickets without the client's lawful basis: anonymise and keep only the phrase (comp:dpdp_act_rules).
Building a headline on one vivid outlier phrase: use phrases that repeat across sources.
Copying slurs, insults or crude language from reviews into brand copy.
how: List sources: the client's reviews (Google, Amazon, Flipkart, Nykaa, app stores), competitors' reviews (3-star ones explain what is missing), support tickets and WhatsApp chats (anonymised, with permission), sales-call recordings, Reddit and Quora threads, YouTube and Instagram comments, open-ended survey answers, customer interviews.
Copy phrases verbatim into a sheet with source and date. Do not paraphrase, fix spelling or translate at this stage; keep Hinglish as typed.
Tag each phrase: pain, trigger moment, desired outcome, what they tried before, objection, words for the product.
Count repeats; phrases that appear in several sources become headline and hook candidates.
Use the customer's words where the reader decides whether to keep reading (headline, hook, subject line, FAQ question); keep the brand voice for explanation and proof.
Re-mine for each new segment or every few months; words change with seasons, prices and competitors.
cards.before: Experience effortless hair care with our nourishing formulation.
cards.after: Monsoon mein baal jhaadu ban jaate hain? Two drops after your wash, and they stay soft till evening.
overuse_signs: Copy so full of customer slang that it no longer matches the brand
Every headline is a lightly edited review quote
Spelling and grammar errors copied in for 'authenticity'
A research sheet of 500 phrases that never reaches the copy

sources.title: Voice of the customer (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: capturing customers' expressed needs in their own terms

cards.name: Vulnerability / confession
cards.summary: Admit a real, specific mistake, fear or failure (what happened, what it cost, what you did wrong) before the lesson, so the reader trusts the advice that follows. Good confession is plain and factual, owns the writer's part, and ends on something useful to the reader rather than a request for sympathy.
use_for: founder and leader posts on LinkedIn and in newsletters
about pages and brand stories (why the company exists)
personal essays and talks
coaching and course content, where the teacher's past mistake is the lesson
client case studies told from the agency's side ('what we got wrong in month one')
avoid: Invented or inflated struggle ('I cried when we hit 10k followers'): readers spot it and trust drops. If there is no real story, use a client story or plain advice.
Humblebrags dressed as confession ('My biggest flaw is caring too much'): name an actual cost.
Crisis statements and apologies: readers want ownership and action, not the leader's feelings; use genre:apology_statement structure.
Other people's private details (an employee's illness, a client's name) without their permission.
how: Pick a real failure directly connected to the lesson or offer; if the link needs explaining, pick another.
Get the specifics from the person (when ghostwriting, interview them): what happened, when, what it cost in rupees, months, clients or relationships, and what they did wrong.
Tell it early and in the first person, in plain words; let the facts carry the emotion instead of adjectives ('devastating', 'rock bottom').
Own the writer's part; do not blame the market, the team or luck.
Show what changed: the specific practice or rule the person follows now.
End with what the reader can use, not with a request for comfort or likes.
Before publishing, ask the person: 'Are you comfortable with a client or investor reading this?'
cards.before: As a founder, I've faced many challenges, but every failure taught me valuable lessons that made me stronger.
cards.after: In 2023 I lost our biggest client, a Ludhiana hosiery brand, because I promised a 10-day turnaround I knew we couldn't hit. We missed it by three weeks. Now every quote we send has two dates: the one we expect and the one we guarantee.
overuse_signs: Every post opens with 'I failed' or 'I was broke'
The same arc every time: struggle, tears, breakthrough, link in bio
Emotional words with no facts (no dates, amounts or names)
Lessons that do not follow from the story told

sources.title: Confessional writing (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: the confessional mode in literature (the marketing use is a craft extension)

cards.name: Writing to a word budget
cards.summary: Before drafting, split the brief's total length into a budget per section, weighted by how much work each section does, and write next to the outline headings; when the draft runs over, cut whole points from the section that overspent instead of shaving words evenly. Good budgeting lands the piece on length with the most words where the reader decides.
use_for: blog posts, articles and guides with a commissioned word count
scripts with a fixed duration (convert seconds to words at the measured speaking pace)
cold emails, ads and captions with hard platform limits
proposals, grant applications and award entries with per-section limits
briefing other writers (budgets in the content brief)
avoid: Padding a section to hit its number: a budget is a ceiling, not a target; finish short and say so if the content is complete.
Budgeting the zero draft: draft freely first if you are still finding the argument, then budget at revision (tech:zero_draft).
Equal budgets for unequal jobs: the section that proves or explains the core point gets the most words.
Budgeting scripts in words from a guess: time a read-aloud at the real pace (and in the real language, since Hindi and English run differently) and budget from that.
how: Take the total from the brief, the platform limit (plat: cards) or the duration. For video and audio, time yourself or the voice reading a sample paragraph and convert seconds to words.
List the sections from the outline (tech:outlining).
Mark the one or two sections that do the main job (the answer, the proof, the offer) and give them the largest share; keep openers and CTAs short.
Write the number next to each heading: 'Hook + answer 80 / Who needs it 120 / Steps 300 / Costs 180 / Mistakes 80 / CTA 40'.
Draft; check each section against its budget when you finish it, not at the end.
When a section overruns, decide: does it deserve the words (take them from a weaker section) or does it need a cut?
Cut whole items first (a second example, a repeated point, a tangent), then sentences, then words (edit:cut_ten_percent).
Do a final count against the total and any hard platform limit.
cards.before: 800-word brief: intro drafted first and runs 310 words; the full draft hits 1,240, gets trimmed by deleting adjectives everywhere, and still ends at 1,050.
cards.after: 800-word plan: Hook + answer 80 / Who needs it 120 / Steps 300 / Costs and timelines 180 / Mistakes 80 / CTA 40. Draft lands at 860; the second mistakes example goes; final 805.
overuse_signs: Sections padded to reach their allotment
Every section the same length whatever its importance
Key proof or a needed step cut to save 20 words
Word counts checked obsessively during the first draft

cards.name: Wordplay and puns
cards.summary: Use a double meaning or a sound-alike to earn a smile, in one high-visibility line, only where the brand voice allows it and the line still makes literal sense to someone who misses the joke. Good wordplay is tied to the product and survives translation into the audience's actual language.
use_for: taglines, shop names and campaign lines
headlines, reel on-screen text and meme captions
festival and topical posts (moment marketing)
packaging and menu copy for playful brands
avoid: Serious or sensitive copy (condolences, health risks, money warnings, crisis statements, civic safety): write plainly.
Cross-language puns for an audience that speaks only one of the languages (a Hindi-English pun in a Tamil or Bengali campaign): test with a reader from the target audience.
Puns whose second meaning touches caste, religion, gender, bodies or a region: check the other reading with someone from that group, and drop it if in doubt.
Puns on a competitor's or celebrity's name or mark: legal risk (comp:trade_marks_comparative_ads) and easy backlash; play on your own product instead.
Puns in CTAs, instructions, error messages or prices: clarity first.
how: Write the plain line first, with the exact meaning you need.
List the product's own words (ingredients, actions, place, category) and brainstorm their double meanings, sound-alikes and idioms.
Keep a pun only if the line still reads as a true, sensible statement to someone who does not get the joke.
Use one pun per piece, in the headline, tagline or on-screen text, not in the body.
For Hinglish wordplay, check that the target reader actually code-switches that way, and read it aloud in their accent.
Read the second meaning on purpose and ask whether it could offend or mislead.
If you have to explain it, drop it and go back to the plain line.
cards.before: Our bakery has made fresh bread in Bandra since 1987.
cards.after: Bandra's bread winners since 1987.
overuse_signs: A pun in every headline and caption, so the brand reads as a joke account
Two or three puns stacked in one line
Puns explained in brackets or followed by 'see what we did there?'
Wordplay that changes the meaning of the claim

sources.title: Pun (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and types of pun

cards.name: Writing for voice-over
cards.summary: Write for the ear: short sentences with one idea per breath, who before what, numbers rounded and written the way they are said, few abbreviations, present tense, and pronunciation help for hard names. A good VO script sounds like a person talking when read cold at performance pace, and adds what the picture cannot show.
use_for: reels, shorts and explainer video scripts
radio spots, podcast ad reads and IVR prompts
news bulletins and documentary narration
brand films and TVCs
scripts that will be voiced by TTS or a cloned voice
avoid: Reading a print article aloud as VO: rewrite it; long clauses, brackets and exact figures that work on paper trip the voice and lose the listener.
VO that repeats the on-screen text word for word: split the jobs (tech:onscreen_text_vs_vo).
Rounding a number whose exact value matters (a refund amount, a deadline, a helpline number): keep it exact and say it slowly, or put it on screen too.
Describing what the viewer can already see ('Here you can see a farmer in a field'): say what the picture cannot.
how: Write one idea per sentence, short enough to say in one breath; broadcast guidance keeps spoken sentences to about 20 words or fewer.
Put attribution and titles before the claim and the name: 'Police say...', 'District collector Anita Rao...'.
Write numbers as they will be said and round them unless the exact figure matters: 'nearly two thousand', 'about thirteen hundred crore rupees', 'saadhe chaar crore' in a Hindi script.
Spell out or drop abbreviations unless the audience says them as letters (GST, UPI). Write symbols as words (per cent, rupees).
Add pronunciation help in brackets for hard names and places, and check names against how the person or place says them.
Use present tense and active voice where you can; avoid semicolons, brackets and long parentheticals. Use full stops and line breaks to mark pauses.
Read it aloud at performance pace with a timer. Rewrite any line where you run out of breath, stumble or lose the thread.
For TTS voices, listen to every line once: check numbers, names, Hindi words in Roman script and the first word of each line.
cards.before: The scheme, launched by the state's Department of Rural Development (DRD) in 2024 with an outlay of Rs 1,284.6 crore, provides solar pumps; beneficiaries, as per the 2023 survey, are selected by the gram sabha.
cards.after: Who gets a solar pump? Your gram sabha decides. Not an officer. Not an agent. The state has set aside about thirteen hundred crore rupees for these pumps.
overuse_signs: Every line a fragment, so the script sounds like a telegram
Rhetorical questions every few seconds to sound conversational
Exact figures rounded so far that the claim becomes vague or wrong
Scripts written for the ear but published unchanged as the caption

sources.title: UF/IFAS EDIS WC193: News Writing for Television and Radio
sources.supports: read the story aloud; sentences of 20 words or less; round numbers unless the exact number is significant; attribution before the quote; avoid most abbreviations; present tense (read 2026-10-05)

sources.title: Media Helping Media: Writing a radio news script
sources.supports: one idea per sentence, one breath; simplify figures; titles before names; phonetic spellings for difficult names; avoid semicolons and colons; read aloud (read 2026-10-05)

sources.title: Voice-over (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: what voice-over narration is

cards.name: You-focus (second person)
cards.summary: Address the reader as 'you' and make them the subject of the sentence, so the copy is about what they get and do; keep 'we' for what the organisation promises and owns. Good you-focused copy answers 'what does this mean for me?' in every paragraph without assuming things about the reader that may not be true.
use_for: landing pages, service pages and product pages
emails, WhatsApp broadcasts and SMS
government and scheme explainers (what you get, what you must do)
help articles and instructions
proposals, where the client's situation should lead
avoid: Blaming 'you' in error and warning messages ('You entered the wrong PIN'): describe the problem and the fix ('That PIN doesn't match. Try again.').
Dodging the brand's own responsibility by making the reader the subject ('You will be refunded'): say 'We'll refund you within 5 working days'.
Assumptions about the reader's life or feelings ('You're tired of your dead-end job'): describe the situation and let the reader opt in ('If your job...').
House styles that require third person (academic papers, some legal documents): follow the style.
how: Mark every sentence whose subject is the company ('We are', 'Our team', 'We offer'). Count them against 'you' sentences.
For each, ask what the reader gets or does because of it, and rewrite with the reader as the subject: 'We offer 24x7 support' becomes 'You can reach a person at 2 am'.
Keep 'we' where the organisation makes a promise or owns a problem: 'We'll call you back within an hour', 'We got this wrong'.
Pick one form of address and keep it: don't switch between 'you', 'users', 'customers' and 'one'.
In Hindi and Hinglish, choose aap, tum or tu for the brand and audience and never mix them; aap is the safe default for government, banks, healthcare and older readers.
Use 'you' instead of 'he or she' to avoid gendering the reader.
Read each paragraph as the reader and ask 'so what for me?' (tech:so_what_test).
cards.before: We are a leading Pune-based logistics company. We offer same-day delivery and we have a fleet of 120 vans.
cards.after: Book by noon and your parcel leaves Pune the same day, on one of our 120 vans.
overuse_signs: 'You' in every sentence, so the copy sounds like a sales script
Sentences that tell the reader what they feel or want
The brand never says 'we' even when it should take responsibility
'Aap' and 'tum' mixed in the same piece

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use the right tone
sources.supports: address the user as 'you' where possible

sources.title: GOV.UK A to Z style guide
sources.supports: address the user as 'you'; avoid gendered pronouns

cards.name: Zero draft (permission to write badly)
cards.summary: Write a complete rough version start to finish without stopping to edit, polish or look things up, marking gaps in brackets, then revise in separate passes. The idea is popularised by Anne Lamott's 'shitty first drafts' chapter in Bird by Bird; a good zero draft is fast, planned and private, never the version anyone else sees.
use_for: long pieces: articles, white papers, reports, scripts, book chapters
pieces where the writer is stuck on the first line
ghostwriting, after the interview, to get the person's story down while it is fresh
getting your own angle and specifics on the page before using an AI tool to help revise
avoid: Sending the zero draft to a client or editor: it is for you; revise before anyone sees it.
Using it to skip research on factual pieces: research and outline first, then draft fast, marking anything unchecked.
Very short pieces (a push notification, a subject line): write several options and pick; there is nothing to 'draft through'.
Leaving placeholders unresolved: every [TK] must be filled from a source before revision ends (edit:fact_check).
how: Prepare first: brief, a short outline (even five bullets), research notes and a rough word budget.
Set a timer and close other tabs; decide to reach the end, not to make it good.
Write from the first section to the last without rereading, deleting or fixing.
When you hit a gap, mark it and keep going: [TK: client count], [CHECK: penalty amount], [better example].
Let the language come as it comes (Hinglish thoughts included) and fix register later.
If you think of a better opening or ending, write it in brackets and keep going.
Stop at the end; step away for an hour or a night.
Revise in passes, in order: structure (edit:developmental_edit), facts (fill every bracket), lines (edit:line_edit), then proofread.
cards.before: Writes the first line, rewrites it nine times, stops to check a GST rate, rewrites the intro again; after 50 minutes, 120 words.
cards.after: 45 minutes, door closed: 1,050 rough words from hook to CTA, with [TK: client count] and [CHECK: penalty amount] marked. Tomorrow: structure pass, fill the brackets, then the line edit.
overuse_signs: Endless zero drafts and no finished piece
Rough drafts sent to clients labelled 'just a first pass'
Brackets still in the published piece
Revision that only polishes sentences and never fixes structure

sources.title: Poynter: The power of awful first drafts
sources.supports: case for fast, imperfect first drafts in journalism; discusses Anne Lamott's Bird by Bird and 'shitty first drafts'; separate drafting from critical revision (read 2026-10-05)
